'''Barry Victor Lloyd Potter''' (born 1953)  [[Member of the Academia Europaea|MAE]] [[Fellow of the Academy of Medical Sciences|FMedSci]] is a British chemist, who is Professor of Medicinal & Biological Chemistry<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://pharm.ox.ac.uk/team/barry-v-l-potter|title=Department of Pharmacology, University of Oxford}}</ref> in the [[Department of Pharmacology, University of Oxford|Department of Pharmacology at]] the [[University of Oxford]], [[Wellcome Trust]] Senior Investigator and a [[Fellow]] of [[University College, Oxford]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.univ.ox.ac.uk/academics/barry-potter/|title=Academics|website=University College Oxford}}</ref>

== Early life and education ==
Potter was born in [[Brighton]],  [[Sussex]] and attended [[Blatchington Mill School|Hove County Grammar School]].<ref>{{Cite book |last=Brock |first=William H. |title=Looking Back. Hove County Grammar School for Boys 1936-73 |publisher=Grosvenor House Publishing Ltd |year=2018 |isbn=978-1-78623-155-0 |location=Surrey |pages=247–8 |language=English}}</ref> He won an Open Exhibition scholarship to [[Worcester College, Oxford|Worcester College]], [[University of Oxford]] to study Chemistry and obtained a first class [[Bachelor of Arts]] degree (with a subsequent [[Master of Arts|MA]]), also winning the Part II Thesis Prize in [[Organic chemistry|Organic Chemistry]]. He earned a [[Doctor of Philosophy]] degree<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://solo.bodleian.ox.ac.uk/primo-explore/fulldisplay?docid=oxfaleph016728139&context=L&vid=SOLO&search_scope=LSCOP_ALL&tab=local&lang=en_US|title=An investigation of enzyme mechanisms using substrate analogues|date=1980|website=Bodleian Library, Oxford}}</ref> from [[Wolfson College, Oxford]], where he also won a Graduate Scholarship and was later [[Junior Research Fellow]], for work carried out in the [[Dyson Perrins Laboratory]] on the stereochemistry of [[Enzyme catalyzed reaction|enzyme-catalyzed]] phosphoryl transfer reactions under the supervision of Gordon Lowe FRS.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Stirling |first=C.J.M |title="Gordon Lowe. 31 May 1933 – 6 August 2003: Elected FRS 1984". |url=https://royalsocietypublishing.org/doi/pdf/10.1098/rsbm.2005.0015 |journal=Biographical Memoirs of Fellows of the Royal Society |date=January 2005 |volume=51 |issue=doi:10.1098/rsbm.2005.0015 |pages=237–252 (2005)|doi=10.1098/rsbm.2005.0015 |doi-access=free|s2cid=71053074 |url-access=subscription }}</ref> He was subsequently awarded a [[Doctor of Science|DSc]] degree from the University of Oxford for his published work up to 1992 in ''Studies in [[Biological Chemistry]]''.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://solo.bodleian.ox.ac.uk/primo-explore/fulldisplay?docid=oxfaleph021224060&context=L&vid=SOLO&search_scope=LSCOP_ALL&tab=local&lang=en_US|title=Studies in Biological Chemistry|date=1992|website=Bodleian Library, Oxford}}</ref>

== Career and research ==
Potter was a postdoctoral research associate first at Oxford and subsequently was funded by the [[Royal Society]] to work at the [[Max Planck Institute for Experimental Medicine]] (now [[Max Planck Institute for Multidisciplinary Sciences]]) in [[Göttingen]],  Federal Republic of Germany with [[:de:Fritz Eckstein|Professor Fritz Eckstein]] in the [[nucleic acid]] and [[molecular biology]] fields and he later became a Wissenschaftlicher Mitarbeiter. He was lecturer in [[biological chemistry]] in the [[Department of Chemistry]] at the [[University of Leicester]], a [[Lister Institute of Preventive Medicine|Lister Institute of Preventive Medicine Research Fellow]]<ref>{{Cite web |title=Former Fellows |url=https://www.lister-institute.org.uk/former-fellows/ |access-date=2022-11-05 |website=Lister Institute |language=en-GB}}</ref> and held the established chair of [[Medicinal chemistry|Medicinal Chemistry]] at [[University of Bath]] for over 20 years, initially as Lister Institute Research Professor, and is currently a [[visiting professor]]. He was visiting professor of medicinal and biological chemistry at the University of Oxford until 2015. His research, primarily employing  [[synthetic organic chemistry]], is highly [[Interdisciplinarity|interdisciplinary]] at the interfaces of Chemistry with Biology and with Medicine and encompasses [[Medicinal chemistry|medicinal]] and [[Biological Chemistry|biological chemistry]], [[chemical biology]] and [[drug design]], discovery and development, especially for [[oncology]] and [[women's health]].

He is particularly known for his enzyme mechanistic work on the [[stereochemistry]] of [[enzyme reaction]]s that transfer [[phosphate group]]s eg [[kinase]]s, [[phosphatase]]s, [[polymerase]]s, [[nuclease]]s etc, pioneering application of synthetic [[Chirality|chiral]] isotopomeric phosphates using both stable [[isotope]]s of <sup>16</sup>O-oxygen in the [<sup>16</sup>O,<sup>17</sup>O,<sup>18</sup>O] - approach, also using the <sup>18</sup>O-isotope in combination with sulphur in the [<sup>16</sup>O,<sup>18</sup>O, S] - approach and the [<sup>16</sup>O,<sup>18</sup>O] - approach for internucleotidic linkages;  and the application of synthetic and biological chemistry techniques to [[cellular signalling]] through the study of the calcium-releasing [[second messengers]] [[inositol trisphosphate]] (IP<sub>3</sub>), cyclic adenosine 5'-diphosphate ribose ([[Cyclic ADP-ribose|cADPR]]), nicotinic acid adenine diphosphate ribose 2'-phosphate ([[Nicotinic acid adenine dinucleotide phosphate|NAADP]]) and [[Adenosine diphosphate ribose|adenosine 5'-diphosphate ribose]] (ADPR) and also more widely in [[nucleotide]] and [[carbohydrate]] chemistry.

In his [[drug design]] and discovery work one of the academically discovered "first-in-class" clinical drug targets identified was [[steroid sulfatase|steroid sulfatase (STS)]]<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Thomas |first=MP, Potter BVL |date=2015|title=Discovery and Development of the Aryl O-Sulfamate Pharmacophore for Oncology and Women's Health|journal=J. Med. Chem.|volume=58|issue=19 |pages=7634–58|doi=10.1021/acs.jmedchem.5b00386|pmc=5159624|pmid=25992880}}</ref> and the first potent inhibitor was designed and synthesized by the Potter research group as the steroidal sulfamate  [[Estrone sulfamate|EMATE]].<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Howarth |first=NM, Purohit A, Reed MJ, Potter BVL |date=1994|title=Estrone sulfamates: potent inhibitors of estrone sulfatase with therapeutic potential |journal=J. Med. Chem. |volume=37|issue=2 |pages=219–221|doi=10.1021/jm00028a002|pmid=8295207 }}</ref> Such synthetic active-site-directed, irreversible, time-dependent steroidal and non-steroidal inactivators of the enzyme progressed to clinical trials <ref>{{Cite journal|last=Potter |first=BVL |date=2018|title=Steroid sulphatase inhibition via aryl sulphamates: clinical progress, mechanism and future prospects|journal=J. Mol. Endocrinol. |volume=61 |issue=2 |pages=T233-252 |doi=10.1530/JME-18-0045 |pmid=29618488|doi-access=free }}</ref> and were translated to the pharmaceutical industry. This work in collaboration with [[Michael J. Reed|Michael J Reed]] lead to  sulfamate-based drugs such as [[Irosustat]] ([[BN83495]], [[STX64]]) <ref>{{Cite web|url=https://pubchem.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/compound/Irosustat#section=Top|title=Irosustat|website=NIH US National Library of Medicine, PubChem Open Chemistry Database}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.chemspider.com/Chemical-Structure.4449897.html|title=Irosustat|website=ChemSpider}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.ebi.ac.uk/chembl/compound/inspect/CHEMBL286738|title=Irosustat|last=CHEMBL286738|website=ChEMBL European Bioinformatics Institute [GB]}}</ref> and [[Estradiol sulfamate|E2MATE]] ([[PGL2001]]) that have completed many [[clinical trial]]s in the UK, Europe, USA and Australia in women's health, including for [[hormone replacement therapy]] and [[endometriosis]],<ref name=":2">{{Cite journal|url=https://clinicaltrials.gov/ct2/show/NCT01631981?term=PGL2001&rank=1|title=PGL2001 Proof of Concept Study in Symptomatic Endometriosis (AMBER)|website=NIH US National Library of Medicine ClinicalTrials.gov|date=2 June 2014}}</ref><ref name=":3">{{Cite journal|last=Pohl |first=O, Bestel E, Gotteland JP |date=2014|title=Synergistic effects of E2MATE and norethindrone acetate on steroid sulfatase inhibition: a randomized phase I proof-of-principle clinical study in women of reproductive age |journal=Reprod. Sci.|volume=21|issue=10 |pages=1256–65 |doi=10.1177/1933719114522526 |pmid=24604234|s2cid=206805308 }}</ref> post-menopausal [[ER+]] hormone dependent [[breast cancer]],<ref name=":4">{{Cite journal|last=Stanway |first=S, Purohit A, Woo LWL, Sufi S, Vigushin D, Ward R, Wilson R, Stanczyk FZ, Dobbs N, Kulinskaya E, Elliott M, Potter BVL, Reed MJ, Coombes RC |date=2006|title=Phase I study of STX64 (667 Coumate) in breast cancer patients: the first study of a steroid sulfatase inhibitor|journal=Clin. Cancer Res.|volume=12|issue=5 |pages=1585–1592|doi=10.1158/1078-0432.CCR-05-1996|pmid=16533785|s2cid=1526070 |doi-access=}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last=Coombes |first=RC, Cardoso F, Isambert N, Lesimple T, Soulié P, Peraire C, Fohanno V, Kornowska A, Ali T, Schmid P |date=2013|title=A phase I dose escalation study to determine the optimal biological dose of irosustat, an oral steroid sulfatase inhibitor, in postmenopausal women with estrogen receptor-positive breast cancer|journal=Breast Cancer Res. Treat.|volume=140|issue=1 |pages=73–82|doi=10.1007/s10549-013-2597-8|pmid=23797179|s2cid=20060727 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |url=https://clinicaltrials.gov/ct2/show/NCT01840488?term=irosustat&rank=3|title=BN83495 Phase I in Post-menopausal Women|website=NIH US National Library of Medicine ClinicalTrials.gov|date=21 November 2019}}</ref><ref name=":0">{{Cite journal|last=Palmieri|first=C, Stein RC, Liu X, Hudson E, Nicholas H, Sasano H, Guestini F, Holcombe C, Barrett S, Kenny L, Reed S, Lim A, Hayward L, Howell S, Coombes RC; IRIS trial participants |date=2017|title=IRIS study: a phase II study of the steroid sulfatase inhibitor Irosustat when added to an aromatase inhibitor in ER-positive breast cancer patients|journal=Breast Cancer Res. Treat. |volume=165 |issue=2 |pages=343–353|doi=10.1007/s10549-017-4328-z |pmid=28612226 |pmc=5543190}}</ref><ref name=":1">{{Cite journal|last=Palmieri|first=C, Szydlo R, Miller M, Barker L, Patel NH, Sasano H, Barwick T, Tam H, Hadjiminas D, Lee J, Shaaban A, Nicholas H, Coombes RC, Kenny LM |date=2017|title=IPET study: an FLT-PET window study to assess the activity of the steroid sulfatase inhibitor irosustat in early breast cancer|journal=Breast Cancer Res. Treat.|volume=166|issue=2 |pages=527–539 |doi=10.1007/s10549-017-4427-x|pmid=28795252|pmc=5668341}}</ref> advanced/metastatic or recurrent estrogen receptor-positive [[endometrial cancer]]<ref>{{Cite journal |url=https://clinicaltrials.gov/ct2/show/NCT00910091?term=irosustat&rank=7|title=Study of Oral Steroid Sulphatase Inhibitor BN83495 Versus Megestrol Acetate (MA) in Women With Advanced or Recurrent Endometrial Cancer|website=NIH US National Library of Medicine ClinicalTrials.gov|date=11 January 2019}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last=Pautier|first=P, Vergote I, Joly F, Melichar B, Kutarska E, Hall G, Lisyanskaya A, Reed N, Oaknin A, Ostapenko V, Zvirbule Z, Chetaille E, Geniaux A, Shoaib M, Green JA |date=2017|title=A Phase 2, Randomized, Open-Label Study of Irosustat Versus Megestrol Acetate in Advanced Endometrial Cancer|journal=Int. J. Gynecol. Cancer|volume=27|issue=2 |pages=258–266|doi=10.1097/igc.0000000000000862|pmid=27870712|s2cid=3430946 |url=https://lirias.kuleuven.be/handle/123456789/558056 |doi-access=free}}</ref> and [[castration-resistant prostate cancer]]<ref>{{Cite journal|url=https://clinicaltrials.gov/ct2/show/NCT00790374?term=irosustat&rank=4|title=BN83495 in Prostate Cancer (STX64PC)|website=NIH US National Library of Medicine ClinicalTrials.gov|date=11 January 2019}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last=Denmeade|first=S, George D, Liu G, Peraire C, Geniaux A, Baton F, Ali T, Chetaille E |date=2011|title=A phase I pharmacodynamics dose escalation study of steroid sulphatase inhibitor Irosustat in patients with prostate cancer|journal=Eur. J. Cancer|volume=47|pages=S499|doi=10.1016/S0959-8049(11)71998-0}}</ref> and Irosustat was also evaluated as a combination therapy with an oral [[epidermal growth factor receptor]] [[tyrosine kinase inhibitor]] for the Treatment of [[Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer]] Patients.<ref>{{Cite web|last=|title=A Pilot Study of a Steroid Sulphatase Inhibitor (BN83495) in Patients Receiving an Oral Epidermal Growth Factor Receptor Tyrosine Kinase Inhibitor (EGFR-TKI) for the Treatment of Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer (NSCLC)|url=https://www.anzctr.org.au/Trial/Registration/TrialReview.aspx?id=336296|url-status=live|website=Australian New Zealand Clinical Trials Registry|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200815173333/https://anzctr.org.au/Trial/Registration/TrialReview.aspx?id=336296 |archive-date=2020-08-15 }}</ref> Irosustat is still progressing clinically. E2MATE/PGL2001 was well tolerated and for [[endometriosis]] first clinical trials showed that local endometrial STS could be reduced by 91% by a single dose of only 4&nbsp;mg/per week of the drug alone and 96% in combination with a progestin.<ref name=":3" /> A Phase II, multicentre, randomised, two-arm, parallel group, double-blind, placebo controlled, clinical study was initiated at 20 clinical centres in Hungary, Romania and Poland.<ref name=":2" /> Results are awaited. In randomised phase II trials using Irosustat ''vs'' the current standard of care (megestrol acetate) in recurrent/metastatic post-menopausal endometrial cancer patients results showed clinical activity and a good safety profile. Pharmacodynamic proof of concept for Irosustat was demonstrated in prostate cancer patients with suppression of the non-sulfated androgens [[testosterone]], [[androstenediol]] and [[DHEA]]. The most recent IRIS <ref>{{Cite journal|url=https://clinicaltrials.gov/ct2/show/NCT01785992|title=A Study of the Safety and Effectiveness of Irosustat When Added to an AI in ER+ve Locally Advanced or Metastatic Breast Cancer. (IRIS)|website=NIH US National Library of Medicine ClinicalTrials.gov|date=23 March 2015}}</ref> and IPET <ref>{{Cite journal|url=https://clinicaltrials.gov/ct2/show/NCT01662726|title=A Study to Assess the Ability of a Novel Endocrine Treatment for Breast Cancer, Irosustat, to Slow Down Cancer Growth (IPET)|website=NIH US National Library of Medicine ClinicalTrials.gov|date=11 March 2016}}</ref> breast cancer clinical trials <ref name=":0" /><ref name=":1" /> met their clinical endpoints; results were discussed <ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.cancerresearchuk.org/about-cancer/find-a-clinical-trial/a-study-looking-irosustat-early-breast-cancer#undefined|title=A study looking at irosustat for early breast cancer (IPET)|website=Cancer Research UK|date=17 March 2015}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.cancerresearchuk.org/about-cancer/find-a-clinical-trial/a-study-looking-irosustat-treat-advanced-breast-cancer-iris#undefined|title=A study looking at irosustat to treat advanced breast cancer (IRIS)|website=Cancer Research UK|date=17 March 2015}}</ref> and clinical benefit demonstrated for Irosustat both as a monotherapy in early breast cancer and in combination with an [[aromatase inhibitor]]. Further trials are necessary.

Potter co-founded in 1997 the university spin-out company Sterix Limited <ref>{{Cite web|url=https://beta.companieshouse.gov.uk/company/03337831|title=Sterix Ltd|website=Companies House}}</ref> jointly between the [[University of Bath]] and [[Imperial College London|Imperial College, London]] and was Director of Medicinal Chemistry and [[Chief scientific officer|Chief Scientific Officer]].  Sterix Ltd pioneered ''inter alia'' the first human clinical trials of a steroid sulfatase inhibitor in breast cancer patients <ref name=":4" /> and was acquired by the French [[Ipsen Group]] in 2004.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.industriepharma.fr/pharmacie-ipsen-acquiert-le-britannique-sterix,29459|title=Pharmacie : Ipsen acquiert le britannique Sterix|date=2004|last1=Nouvelle|first1=L'Usine|access-date=27 February 2019|archive-date=25 September 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200925121552/https://www.industriepharma.fr/pharmacie-ipsen-acquiert-le-britannique-sterix,29459|url-status=dead}}</ref>

It has been demonstrated that oral treatment with the STS inhibitor [[Irosustat]] alleviates the symptoms of [[Alzheimer's disease]] in a murine model, indicating that the drug passes the [[blood–brain barrier]]. STS inhibitors could therefore potentially be employed to treat such ageing and ageing-associated diseases, including Huntington’s and Parkinson’s diseases.<ref>{{Cite journal|date=2021|title=Steroid hormones sulfatase inactivation extends lifespan and ameliorates age-related diseases|journal=Nature Communications|volume=12|pages=49|doi=10.1038/s41467-020-20269-y|doi-access=free|pmid=33397961|last1=Pérez-Jiménez|first1=M. M.|last2=Monje-Moreno|first2=J. M.|last3=Brokate-Llanos|first3=A. M.|last4=Venegas-Calerón|first4=M.|last5=Sánchez-García|first5=A.|last6=Sansigre|first6=P.|last7=Valladares|first7=A.|last8=Esteban-García|first8=S.|last9=Suárez-Pereira|first9=I.|last10=Vitorica|first10=J.|last11=Ríos|first11=J. J.|last12=Artal-Sanz|first12=M.|last13=Muñoz|first13=M. J.|issue=1|pmc=7782729|bibcode=2021NatCo..12...49P}}</ref> The Spanish spin-out company  ONESTX <ref>{{Cite web |last=ONESTX |title=ONSTX |url=https://onestx.bio/}}</ref> will pursue clinical application to such pathologies with STX64/Irosustat, both alone and in combination with neurosteroids.

Because of dual effects on stimulation of bone formation and inhibition of bone resorption Nexyon Biotech (Korea) is taking sulfatase inhibition into phase 2 clinical trials for ''osteogenesis imperfecta'' <ref>{{Cite web |last=Nexyon Biotech |title=Nexyonbio Development Pipeline |url=https://www.nexyonbio.com/eng/research/pipeline.php}}</ref>

In 2020-2021 a themed journal issue was dedicated to Professor Potter entitled: "From Cell Signalling to Anticancer Drug Discovery".<ref>{{Cite journal|editor1=M Migaud |editor2=G Wagner|title=Special Issue "From Cell Signalling to Anticancer Drug Discovery: A Theme Issue in Honor of Professor Barry Potter"|url=https://www.mdpi.com/journal/molecules/special_issues/theme_barry_potter|journal=Molecules|volume=25-26}}</ref>

As of 2025, Potter has published more than 550 articles in peer-reviewed journals, with many of his papers appearing in highly selective journals and is inventor of 45 granted US patents. His work has been cited ca. 25,000 times and he has an h-index of 78 and an i10 index of 440.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Barry V L Potter |url=https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=0XhDZiIAAAAJ&hl=en |access-date=2026-08-04 |website=scholar.google.com}}</ref>

== Awards and honours ==
Potter is a [[Fellow of the Royal Society of Chemistry]] (FRSC)  and [[Fellow of the Royal Society of Biology]] (FRSB).

He was elected a Fellow of the [[Academy of Medical Sciences, United Kingdom|Academy of Medical Sciences]] ([[FMedSci]]) in 2008.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://acmedsci.ac.uk/fellows/fellows-directory/ordinary-fellows/fellow/Professor-Barry-Potter-0006352|title=Ordinary Fellows|website=Academy of Medical Sciences}}</ref> The citation reads:
{{blockquote|He has made wide-ranging contributions at the interface of Chemistry with both Biology and Medicine. In [[Chemical biology|Chemical Biology]] he has elucidated the [[stereochemistry]] of numerous enzyme-catalysed phosphoryl and nucleotidyl transfer reactions using isotopically chiral substrates and DNA fragments. He has applied [[organic synthesis]] techniques in novel ways using carbohydrate, cyclitol and phosphorus chemistry to design modulators of cellular signal transduction processes that mobilize intracellular Ca<sup>2+</sup> through second messengers. Of particular relevance to this Academy he has pioneered the novel aryl sulfamate pharmacophore in drug design. Unusually within an academic setting, he has brought compounds from initial academic concept to multiple [[clinical trial]]s in women's health. These have shown evidence of efficacy in humans, particularly in the anti-cancer field related to hormone-dependent breast cancer.}}

He was elected a Member ([[Member of the Academia Europaea|MAE]]) of the pan-European Academy of Science, Humanities & Letters the ''[[Academia Europaea]]''  in 2009.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.ae-info.org/ae/Acad_Main/List_of_Members/ListMembersBySection?type=listsection&pagenr=800|title=Academy of Europe|website=Chemical Sciences Section}}</ref>

He has also won a number of academic and industrial awards and medals e.g.: [[Royal Society of Chemistry]], 2007 UCB-Celltech Industrially Sponsored Award & Medal  for Chemical Biology;<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.rsc.org/ScienceAndTechnology/Awards/Archive/ChemicalBiology/Index.asp|title=Chemical Biology Award|website=Royal Society of Chemistry}}</ref> [[Royal Society of Chemistry]], 2007/8 sulphatase inhibitors recognised with GSK In 2022 Potter was awarded the degree of [[Doctor of Science]] ''[[honoris causa]]'' by the [[University of Bath]]<ref>{{Cite web |last=University of Bath |date=June 2022 |title=Professor Stephen Ward's oration for the honorary degree of Doctor of Science June 2022 |url=https://www.bath.ac.uk/corporate-information/professor-barry-v-l-potter-ma-dphil-dsc-frsb-frsc-mae-fmedsci-oration/}}</ref> and was also elected to an [[Honorary fellowship|Honorary Fellowship]] of the [[British Pharmacological Society]] (HonFBPhS).<ref>{{Cite web |last=British Pharmacological Society |date=1 December 2022 |title=New Fellows and Honorary Fellows for 2022 |url=https://www.bps.ac.uk/news/articles/2022/announces-new-fellows-and-honorary-fellows-for-202}}</ref>
